name: Short histories of BARMM areas
note: A short, neutral history of each province, area, city and municipality, written for its page from the laws that created it (read on Lawphil, ChanRobles or the Bangsamoro Parliament) and from cited general sources. Each lists the sources it rests on. No statistics: the figures are elsewhere on the page.

paragraphs: Basilan is home to the Yakan, its indigenous Muslim people, along with Tausug and Sama communities and Chavacano-speaking Christians who settled from Zamboanga and the Visayas. Spanish forces first attacked the island in 1578. Under American rule, plantations for rubber and copra were established.

Republic Act 288 of 1948 separated Basilan from Zamboanga City and made it a city, joining Isabela with the districts of Lamitan and Maluso. Presidential Decree 356 of 1973 then created the Province of Basilan, with Isabela as its capital. The provincial capital has since moved to Lamitan, which became a city under Republic Act 9393 in 2007.

Basilan voted against joining the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) in 1989. In the 2001 plebiscite under Republic Act 9054, the province joined, but Isabela City did not. In January 2019, Basilan voted to ratify the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act 11054) and became part of the BARMM. Isabela City again voted no, and it remains in the Zamboanga Peninsula region.

paragraphs: Lanao del Sur is the homeland of the Maranao, whose name means "people of the lake", after Lake Lanao. Their society was organised in the Pat a Pangampong ko Ranao, the four confederated states of Unayan, Masiu, Bayabao and Baloi. Maranao culture is known for the torogan royal house, the darangen epic and okir design.

Lanao was one province until Republic Act 2228 of 1959 divided it into Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur. Marawi, renamed from Dansalan by Republic Act 1552 in 1956, became the capital of Lanao del Sur.

In the 1989 plebiscite under Republic Act 6734, Lanao del Sur voted to join the new Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, while Marawi City did not. Marawi joined in the 2001 plebiscite under Republic Act 9054. In January 2019, the province voted to ratify the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act 11054) and became part of the BARMM. In 2017, the Battle of Marawi caused heavy destruction in the city.

sources.label: Republic Act 2228 (1959), Creating the Provinces of Lanao del Norte and Lanao del Sur — Lawphil

paragraphs: Maguindanao del Norte lies in the lower valley of the Rio Grande de Mindanao, the heartland of the Sultanate of Maguindanao. Tradition credits Sharif Kabungsuwan of Johor with bringing Islam to the Maguindanaon around the turn of the 16th century. Sultan Kudarat, who ruled in the 17th century, opened Simuay as a major trading port.

The area was part of the old Province of Cotabato until Presidential Decree 341 of 1973 created the Province of Maguindanao. In 1989 Maguindanao voted to join the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. In 2006 a separate province, Shariff Kabunsuan, was formed in much of this territory, but the Supreme Court voided it in 2008, ruling that only Congress can create provinces.

After voting in 2019 to join the BARMM under Republic Act 11054, Maguindanao was divided in two by Republic Act 11550 of 2021. Voters approved the division in a plebiscite on 17 September 2022. Maguindanao del Norte, with its capital at Datu Odin Sinsuat, took effect on 9 January 2023. Cotabato City lies within the area but is not part of the province.

sources.label: Presidential Decree 341 (1973), Creating the Provinces of North Cotabato, Maguindanao and Sultan Kudarat — Lawphil

paragraphs: Maguindanao del Sur covers much of the upper valley of the Rio Grande de Mindanao. This was the seat of the Sultanate of Buayan, centred at present-day Datu Piang, which competed for dominance with the coastal Sultanate of Maguindanao downriver. Together the two sultanates shaped the history of the Cotabato basin.

The area was part of the old Province of Cotabato until Presidential Decree 341 of 1973 created the Province of Maguindanao, with its capital at Maganoy (now Shariff Aguak). In the 1989 plebiscite under Republic Act 6734, Maguindanao voted to join the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. In January 2019, it voted to ratify the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act 11054) and became part of the BARMM.

Republic Act 11550 of 2021 divided Maguindanao into two provinces. Voters approved the division on 17 September 2022, and Maguindanao del Sur took effect on 9 January 2023, with its capital at Buluan.

paragraphs: Tawi-Tawi is the homeland of the Sama and Bajau, seafaring peoples of the islands south of Sulu. The Bolobok Rock Shelter shows that people lived here thousands of years ago. Tradition holds that in 1380 the Arab missionary Makhdum Karim built a mosque at Simunul, often called the oldest in the Philippines. The islands later came under the Sultanate of Sulu, and then under Spanish rule.

Presidential Decree 302 of 1973 separated eight municipalities from Sulu to create the Province of Tawi-Tawi, citing their distance from Sulu's capital. The first capital was Bato-Bato in Balimbing. Batas Pambansa 24 of 1979 moved it to Bongao.

In the 1989 plebiscite under Republic Act 6734, Tawi-Tawi was one of 4 provinces that voted to form the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. In January 2019, it voted to ratify the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act 11054) and became part of the BARMM.

paragraphs: Cotabato City takes its name from Kuta Wato, "stone fort" in Maguindanaon, the seat of the Sultanate of Maguindanao. The Spanish established a town here in 1861 with the consent of local datus, and in 1903 the Americans made Cotabato a municipality within the Moro Province.

Republic Act 2364 of 1959 turned the Municipality of Cotabato into a chartered city. The city voted against joining the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao in 1989. Even so, the regional government was inaugurated there in 1990, and the city served as the ARMM's seat while remaining outside the region.

In the plebiscite of 21 January 2019, Cotabato City voted to join the new Bangsamoro region under the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act 11054). The city was formally turned over to the BARMM in December 2020 and is now its regional centre. It is independent of the surrounding Province of Maguindanao del Norte.

sources.label: Republic Act 2364 (1959), An Act Creating the City of Cotabato — ChanRobles

paragraphs: The Special Geographic Area is made up of 63 barangays that were once part of Cotabato province, which Presidential Decree 341 of 1973 renamed North Cotabato. On 6 February 2019, 67 barangays in 7 North Cotabato towns voted on joining the new Bangsamoro region under the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act 11054). Of these, 63 voted yes, from Aleosan, Carmen, Kabacan, Midsayap, Pigcawayan and Pikit.

The barangays were turned over to the BARMM in November 2019 and grouped as the Special Geographic Area. In 2023 the Bangsamoro Parliament passed Bangsamoro Autonomy Acts 41 to 48, which grouped the barangays into 8 new municipalities: Kadayangan, Kapalawan, Ligawasan, Malidegao, Nabalawag, Old Kaabakan, Pahamuddin and Tugunan. Voters ratified all 8 in a plebiscite on 13 April 2024.

paragraphs: Akbar was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 193, passed by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly on 20 December 2005. The law separated 9 barangays from the Municipality of Tuburan, among them Sinangkapan and the island barangay of Linongan, and constituted them as a new municipality.

The town is named after Imam Akbar Marani, an Islamic preacher described as a descendant of Kudarat, who landed at Taguime in the 17th century. He later lived in Sinangkapan before moving to Lantawan, where he was buried.

Al-Barka was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 191, passed by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly on 20 December 2005. The law separated 16 barangays from the Municipality of Tipo-Tipo, including Guinanta, Kailih and Bato-Bato, and made them a distinct municipality. Its creation was ratified in a plebiscite held on 22 May 2006, the same day as that for neighbouring Ungkaya Pukan, also carved from Tipo-Tipo.

Hadji Mohammad Ajul was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 192, passed by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly on 20 December 2005 and ratified in a plebiscite on 22 May 2006. The law took 11 barangays from the Municipality of Tuburan, including Sibago Island, to form the new town.
Among the barangays transferred was Tuburan Proper, which the law named as the seat of the new municipality's government.

Hadji Muhtamad was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 200, passed by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly on 22 August 2006. The law separated 10 barangays from the Municipality of Lantawan, including Baluk-Baluk, Dasalan and Sangbay, and constituted them as a distinct and independent municipality.
These were the barangays of Lantawan that lie off Basilan Island. The new town's creation was ratified in a plebiscite held on 25 August 2007.

Lamitan is in the traditional homeland of the Yakan people. Local tradition holds that the name comes from lami-lamihan, a Yakan festive gathering that Spanish visitors are said to have taken for the name of the place. In 1886 Pedro Javier Cuevas, known as Datu Kalun, took leadership of the area and founded the settlement. Lamitan was long a municipal district of Basilan, then part of Zamboanga.

Presidential Decree No. 356 of 1973, which created the Province of Basilan, made Lamitan a regular municipality. Republic Act No. 9393, approved on 15 March 2007 and ratified on 18 June 2007, converted it into a component city. Its cityhood was challenged in the Supreme Court in the League of Cities case and finally upheld in 2011.

Lantawan was created as a municipality by Presidential Decree No. 593, signed on 2 December 1974, which amended the decree creating the Province of Basilan and divided the province into 10 municipalities. The decree set Lantawan's seat at Barangay Tairan.

In 2007, 10 of its barangays that lie off Basilan Island were separated to form the new Municipality of Hadji Muhtamad under Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 200, ratified in a plebiscite on 25 August 2007. Lantawan now consists of its barangays on Basilan Island.

Maluso lies on the southwestern part of Basilan Island and is home to Yakan, Iranun, Banguingui and Tausug communities, along with settlers from Luzon and the Visayas, many of whom arrived during the Commonwealth era. The Maluso River, locally called Subah Maluso, is tied to the town's early history and was a source of fresh water for passing European sailors.

Formerly a municipal district, Maluso was made a regular municipality by Presidential Decree No. 356 of 1973, which created the Province of Basilan. Presidential Decree No. 593 of 1974 kept it among the province's municipalities, with its seat at Barangay Maluso.

Sumisip was created as a municipality by Presidential Decree No. 593, signed on 2 December 1974, which divided the Province of Basilan into 10 municipalities. The decree, which spells the name Sumipsip, set its seat at Barangay Mangal.

Under Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 187, passed in 2007, the islands of Bubuan, Lanawan, Saluping and Tabuan-Lasa, with their 12 barangays, were separated from Sumisip to form the Municipality of Tabuan-Lasa. The change was ratified in a plebiscite on 29 March 2008.

Tabuan-Lasa is an island municipality created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 187, passed by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly in 2007. The law separated the 4 islands of Bubuan, Lanawan, Saluping and Tabuan-Lasa, with their 12 barangays, from the Municipality of Sumisip and made them a distinct municipality.
The law set the seat of government at Barangay Lanawan on Lanawan Island. The creation was ratified in a plebiscite held on 29 March 2008.

Tipo-Tipo was created as a municipality by Presidential Decree No. 593, signed on 2 December 1974, which divided the Province of Basilan into 10 municipalities. The decree set its seat at Barangay Tipo-Tipo.

In 2006 the town was split under 2 laws of the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly: Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 190 created Ungkaya Pukan from 12 of its barangays, and Act No. 191 created Al-Barka from 16 more. Both were ratified in plebiscites on 22 May 2006, leaving Tipo-Tipo with 11 barangays.

Tuburan was created as a municipality by Presidential Decree No. 593, signed on 2 December 1974, which divided the Province of Basilan into 10 municipalities. The decree set its seat at Barangay Tuburan.

2 towns were later carved from it under laws passed by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly in December 2005: Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 192 created Hadji Mohammad Ajul from 11 barangays, including Tuburan Proper, and Act No. 193 created Akbar from 9 more. Tuburan was left with 10 barangays.

Ungkaya Pukan was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 190, passed by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly on 20 December 2005 and ratified in a plebiscite on 22 May 2006. The law separated 12 barangays from the Municipality of Tipo-Tipo, including Amaloy, Matata and Tongbato, to form the new town.
The town is named after Orang Kaya Pukan, a Yakan chieftain who, according to local history, resisted Pedro Javier Cuevas, known as Datu Kalun, and his Spanish-backed forces.

Amai Manabilang was created as the Municipality of Bumbaran by Presidential Decree No. 1243, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 17 November 1977. The decree separated a group of barangays from Wao, which it described as too vast to police, and made Barangay Aparport the seat of government. The old name recalls Bembaran, the legendary kingdom of the Maranao epic Darangen.
Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 316, approved on 22 January 2015, changed the name of Bumbaran to Amai Manabilang. The new name was confirmed in a plebiscite held on 7 April 2018.

Bacolod-Kalawi is a Maranao town that began as the municipal district of Bacolod Grande. It appears under that name in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960, which reclassified the municipal districts of Lanao del Sur, and in Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963, by which President Diosdado Macapagal declared Bacolod Grande and other municipal districts with sufficient revenue to be regular municipalities.
In 1994 the Regional Legislative Assembly of the then Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao passed Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 32, renaming Bacolod Grande as Bacolod-Kalawi.

Balabagan, on the Illana Bay coast, was first organised as a municipality by Executive Order No. 386, signed by President Carlos P. Garcia on 15 March 1960. The order separated barrios including Barorao, Kalilangan, Balabagan, Itil and Banago from Malabang, with the seat of government at Itil.

Congress later passed Republic Act No. 5978, approved on 5 July 1969, which created Balabagan by statute from barrios of Malabang and Dianaton, effective from 16 March 1960, with Barrio Banago as the seat. In 1982 Batas Pambansa Blg. 168 separated a large group of its barangays to form the new municipality of Kapatagan.

Balindong is a Maranao town in an area once known as Watu or Wato, the seat of one of the Maranao sultanates of the lake. Local genealogies trace its ruling families to the founding ancestors of the Masiu principality and link them to the Sultanate of Raya.

Balindong was a municipal district in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960 and was among the Lanao del Sur municipal districts that President Diosdado Macapagal declared regular municipalities through Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963.

Bayang is one of the old Maranao sultanates of the Lake Lanao area. In May 1902, during the Philippine-American War in Mindanao, it was the site of the Battle of Bayang. American troops under Colonel Frank Baldwin attacked the Maranao fortresses (cotta) of Binidayan and Pandapatan after the sultan of Bayang refused to surrender men blamed for an earlier attack. Hundreds of Maranao defenders died, including the sultan of Bayang. The Pandapatan cotta is preserved as a historical monument.
Bayang was a municipal district until Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963 declared it a regular municipality.
Binidayan is a Maranao town near Bayang. Its cotta, or fortress, was the first captured by American troops during the Battle of Bayang in May 1902.

Binidayan was listed as a municipal district in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960. President Diosdado Macapagal declared it a regular municipality through Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963, which covered municipal districts that had earned enough revenue over 4 years. Sultan Raraco Pundag Macaorao served as its first appointed mayor.

Buadiposo-Buntong was created by Presidential Decree No. 1133, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 4 May 1977. The decree separated 32 barangays from Ditsaan-Ramain, among them Buadiposo-Proper, Buntong and Manacab, and made Barangay Manacab the seat of government. It cited economic development and the restoration of peace and order as its reasons.
With Bubong, Ditsaan-Ramain and Kapai, the town is counted in the SHAKBA group of neighbouring municipalities east of Lake Lanao, whose name refers to the rivers that link them.

Bubong is a Maranao town east of Lake Lanao and part of the SHAKBA group of neighbouring municipalities with Buadiposo-Buntong, Ditsaan-Ramain and Kapai. It was a municipal district in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960, and President Diosdado Macapagal declared it a regular municipality through Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963.
In 1971 Republic Act No. 6406 included Bubong in a proposed new Maranaw province carved from eastern Lanao del Sur, but the division never took effect after martial law was declared in 1972.

Butig is one of the oldest Maranao settlements and a sultanate of the Unayan principality. Historians trace its ruling line to the marriage alliances of Sharif Kabungsuwan in the 16th century, and Islam is said to have reached the Lake Lanao Maranao from Butig. A Spanish expedition destroyed the town in 1658.

Butig was a municipal district until Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963, signed by President Diosdado Macapagal, declared it a regular municipality. In 1977 Presidential Decree No. 1091 transferred 4 of its barangays to the new municipality of Lumbayanague.

Calanogas was created by Presidential Decree No. 1132, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 4 May 1977. The decree separated barangays from the municipalities of Pagayawan and Pualas and formed them into a new municipality, with the seat of government at Barangay Calalanoan. It cited residents' requests and the need to speed up development and restore peace and order in the area.

Ditsaan-Ramain is a Maranao town east of Lake Lanao. A municipal district of Ramain is listed in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960 and was declared a regular municipality by Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963. With Bubong, Buadiposo-Buntong and Kapai it forms the SHAKBA group, a Maranao word for links, named for the rivers that connect them.
In 1977 Presidential Decree No. 1133 separated 32 of its barangays to create Buadiposo-Buntong.

Before American rule, Ganassi was part of the traditional Maranao principality of Unayan. Its name is linked to one of the Nine Princesses of Unayan in Maranao tradition. The town is known for the Laguindab torogan, a royal Maranao house that the National Commission for Culture and the Arts once described as the finest example of its type; it survives in damaged condition.

Ganassi was a municipal district until Executive Order No. 411, signed by President Carlos P. Garcia on 18 January 1961, converted it into a municipality on the recommendation of the Lanao del Sur Provincial Board.

Kapai is a Maranao town east of Lake Lanao and part of the SHAKBA group with Bubong, Buadiposo-Buntong and Ditsaan-Ramain. It was a municipal district in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960. Executive Order No. 77, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 18 July 1967, declared Kapai a regular municipality effective 1 July 1964, after it met the revenue requirement.
In 1971 Republic Act No. 6406 included Kapai in a proposed Maranaw province, which was never formed.

Kapatagan was created by Batas Pambansa Blg. 168, approved on 8 February 1982. The law separated a large group of barangays from Balabagan and made the site of Barangay Kapatagan the seat of government, subject to a plebiscite held on 17 May 1982 alongside the barangay elections. Most of its residents speak Iranun, unlike the mainly Maranao-speaking rest of Lanao del Sur.

Lumba-Bayabao is a Maranao town east of Lake Lanao. It was a municipal district until Executive Order No. 428, signed by President Carlos P. Garcia on 1 June 1961, converted it into a municipality on the recommendation of the Lanao del Sur Provincial Board.

In 1971 Republic Act No. 6406 placed Lumba-Bayabao, then including what is now Maguing, in a proposed Maranaw province carved from eastern Lanao del Sur. The division never took effect after martial law was declared in 1972.

Lumbaca-Unayan takes its name from Unayan, one of the traditional Maranao principalities around Lake Lanao. It was created from part of Lumbatan by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 106, signed by Regional Governor Nur Misuari on 22 November 2000. Residents approved its creation in a plebiscite on 27 November 2004.

Lumbatan is a Maranao town in Lanao del Sur. It was a municipal district in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960, and President Diosdado Macapagal declared it a regular municipality through Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963.

Two municipalities were later carved from its territory. Presidential Decree No. 1091 of 1977 transferred 30 of its barangays to the new municipality of Lumbayanague. Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 106 of 2000 created Lumbaca-Unayan from another 9, a change confirmed by plebiscite in 2004.

Lumbayanague was created by Presidential Decree No. 1091, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 14 February 1977. The decree separated 30 barangays from Lumbatan and 4 from Butig and made Barangay Lumbayanague the seat of government. It cited the need to improve law and order and speed up development in the area. In Maranao tradition the name is associated with one of the Nine Princesses of Unayan.

Madalum is a Maranao town in Lanao del Sur. It was a municipal district in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960. Executive Order No. 77, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 18 July 1967, declared it a regular municipality effective 1 July 1964, after its revenue had passed the legal threshold for 4 straight fiscal years.
Residents mark the signing date each year as Araw ng Madalum on 18 July.

Madamba is a Maranao town in Lanao del Sur. In the traditional order of the Lanao sultanates it was one of 4 territories, with Bakayawan, Dalama and Sawer, whose consent was needed to validate the appointment of a new sultan.
Madamba was a municipal district in Executive Order No. 409 of 1960, and President Diosdado Macapagal declared it a regular municipality through Executive Order No. 42 of 25 June 1963.

Maguing was created on 4 May 1977 by Presidential Decree No. 1134, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos. The decree separated a group of barrios from Lumba-Bayabao, which it described as too large for its officials to govern efficiently, and called the new town the rice production centre of the Basak area. Barrio Dilausan was made the seat of government.

The name is older than the town. Until 1956 Maguing was the name of the municipal district that Republic Act No. 1420 renamed Lumba Bayabao. In 2024 a bill was filed in the Bangsamoro Parliament to create a new municipality, Raya Maguing, from 14 of its barangays.

Malabang is a Maranao town with a long history. During the wars against Spain it served as a headquarters of Sultan Muhammad Kudarat of Maguindanao, who later retired there and was buried there. In the Second World War the Japanese built a large camp at Malabang, where Chief Justice José Abad Santos was executed in 1942 for refusing to cooperate; the site is now Camp Jose Abad Santos. The town marks its founding on 1 March 1893.
Two towns were later carved from it: Balabagan, created by Executive Order No. 386 in 1960, and Sultan Gumander, now Picong, created by Presidential Decree No. 1135 in 1977.

Marantao is a Maranao town in Lanao del Sur. Its name is a Malay word, merantau, meaning to set out on a journey, a hunt or an expedition. The town is home to the Kawayan Torogan, the oldest known torogan in the Philippines, a traditional house built for Maranao royal families.

Marantao was a municipal district before it became a regular municipality. Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, declared it and several other Lanao del Sur districts municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962.

Marawi, on Lake Lanao, was long known as Dansalan, from the Maranao word for a meeting or landing place. Spanish forces settled there briefly in 1639 and took the Maranao stronghold only in 1895. Dansalan became a municipality in 1907, and in 1935 Maranao leaders signed the Dansalan Declaration there, asking the United States not to include Mindanao and Sulu in Philippine independence.

Commonwealth Act No. 592 made Dansalan a city in 1940, and Republic Act No. 1552 renamed it Marawi in 1956. It became capital of Lanao del Sur in 1959 and was declared the Islamic City of Marawi in 1980. In 2017 a 5-month siege by militants linked to the Islamic State destroyed much of the city centre.

Marogong began as a barangay of Tubaran. Presidential Decree No. 1131, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 4 May 1977, separated 27 barangays from Tubaran to form the Municipality of Marogong, citing Tubaran's large territory, and made Marogong Proper the seat of government. Local accounts credit Sultan Abdulmadid P. Maruhom with settling the area in 1954; he became the town's first appointed mayor and, in 1980, its first elected mayor.

Masiu shares its name with the old Maranao state of Masiu, whose seat before American rule was at present-day Taraka, where the royal title of Sultan sa Masiu is still confirmed. It was a municipal district before it became a regular municipality: Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, declared Masiu and several other Lanao del Sur districts municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962.

Mulondo is a Maranao town in Lanao del Sur whose name is said to come from a Maranao phrase meaning "people of the lake". It was a municipal district before it became a regular municipality: Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, listed it as Molundo among the Lanao del Sur districts declared municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962.

Pagayawan began as the municipal district of Tatarikan. Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, declared Tatarikan and several other Lanao del Sur districts municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962. Republic Act No. 3624, approved on 22 June 1963, changed its name from Tatarikan to Pagayawan. Local tradition links the town to the Nine Princesses of Unayan, an old Maranao lineage.

Piagapo was once part of Saguiaran. Executive Order No. 431, issued on 9 June 1961, divided the municipal district of Saguiaran in two and created the municipal district of Piagapo. Executive Order No. 166, signed on 27 August 1965, declared Piagapo a regular municipality.

Local tradition holds that the land was ruled in early times by a queen, Dayang Labi, known as the Bai sa Radapan and said to descend from Sharif Kabungsuan; the barangay of Radapan bears her title. The name Piagapo was proposed by leaders from Sendigan and adopted for the new district.

Picong was created as the Municipality of Sultan Gumander by Presidential Decree No. 1135, signed on 4 May 1977, which separated a group of barangays from Malabang and made Barangay Liangan the seat of government. The area includes the grave of Sultan Muhammad Kudarat of Maguindanao, who retired to Malabang late in life.
The town was renamed Picong under Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 175, enacted by the ARMM Regional Legislative Assembly. The change was ratified in a plebiscite on 25 March 2006.

Poona Bayabao was first known as the municipal district of Gata. Republic Act No. 1421, approved on 10 June 1956, changed its name to Poona Bayabao. Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, then declared it and several other Lanao del Sur districts regular municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962.

Pualas is a Maranao town in Lanao del Sur, with a predominantly Muslim population. It was a municipal district before it became a regular municipality: Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, declared Pualas and several other Lanao del Sur districts municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962.

Saguiaran, next to Marawi, began as a municipal district. In 1952 Executive Order No. 505 abolished the neighbouring district of Sungud and annexed it to Saguiaran, and in 1961 Executive Order No. 431 split off its western part as the district of Piagapo. Executive Order No. 42, issued in 1963, declared Saguiaran a municipality with effect from 1 July 1962.
The town hosts the Agus II hydroelectric plant, and Lake Pantao Raya and its surroundings were declared a national park in 1965.

Sultan Dumalondong was created in 1995 by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 36, passed by the Regional Legislative Assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. It was formed from parts of 3 neighbouring towns: 3 barangays and 6 sitios from Butig, 1 barangay and 9 sitios from Lumbatan, and 9 barangays and 8 sitios from Lumbayanague.

Tagoloan was created by Presidential Decree No. 1548, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 11 June 1978, which separated 39 barangays from Kapai to form a new municipality with its seat at Barangay Tagoloan. It is listed as Tagoloan II to tell it apart from the towns of the same name in Lanao del Norte and Misamis Oriental.
Local history traces the name to Sharif Alawi, remembered as founder of a Sultanate of Tagoloan around 1500; the name is read as a Maranao compound of tago, the inhabitants, and oloan, the leader.

Tamparan, a Maranao town beside Lake Lanao, takes its name from the Maranao word for frontage. It was a municipal district until Executive Order No. 405, issued on 28 September 1960, converted it into a regular municipality. It is officially styled the Islamic Municipality of Tamparan.

On 12 September 1942, the first day of Ramadan, Japanese soldiers pursuing a Maranao guerrilla leader shelled a fort in the town. Residents armed with bladed farm tools attacked them in what became known as the Battle of Tamparan, killing most of the soldiers at a heavy cost in local lives.

Before American rule, Taraka was the seat of the state of Masiu, one of the traditional Maranao states around Lake Lanao, and the royal title of Sultan sa Masiu is still confirmed there. The town is also home to the Baab-Ur Rahman mosque, regarded as one of the oldest in the country.

Taraka was a municipal district before it became a regular municipality: Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, declared it and several other Lanao del Sur districts municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962.

Before American rule, Tubaran was part of the state of Unayan, one of the traditional Maranao states, and local tradition takes its name from one of the Nine Princesses of Unayan. It was a municipal district until Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, declared it a municipality with effect from 1 July 1962.
In 1977 Presidential Decree No. 1131 separated 27 of its barangays to form the Municipality of Marogong.

Tugaya is known for its Maranao crafts: brass casting, gong making, wood carving, weaving and metalwork decorated with the traditional okir motif. Nearly every household practises one of these crafts, which has earned the town the name Industrial Capital of Lanao del Sur.

Tugaya was a municipal district before it became a regular municipality: Executive Order No. 42, issued on 25 June 1963, declared it and several other Lanao del Sur districts municipalities with effect from 1 July 1962.

Wao grew out of a resettlement programme of the Land Settlement and Development Corporation under President Ramon Magsaysay in the 1950s. The first 60 settler families, from the then undivided Cotabato province, were welcomed by the local Muslim community led by Sultan Mamaco Saripada, who became the first mayor. Executive Order No. 418, issued on 22 February 1961, converted the municipal district of Wao into a municipality.
In 1977 Presidential Decree No. 1243 separated 21 barangays from Wao to form Bumbaran, now Amai Manabilang. Wao is the only town in Lanao del Sur with a Christian majority.

Barira is one of the towns of the Iranun people in the uplands of northern Maguindanao. It was created by Presidential Decree No. 1188, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos in 1977, which detached 10 barangays and dozens of sitios from Buldon and set the seat of government at Sitio Pedtad in Barangay Lipawan.

Before it became a town, part of the area hosted a resettlement farm opened by the Economic Development Corporation for former Huk rebels. Barira later became the site of Camp Abubakar, the main camp of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, which fell to government forces in July 2000 after months of fighting.

Buldon is one of the towns of the Iranun people in northern Maguindanao. It was created by Republic Act No. 3419, approved on 18 June 1961, which separated 12 barrios and 20 sitios from Parang, then in Cotabato province, with the seat of government at Nabalawag. In 1977 Presidential Decree No. 1188 carved the new town of Barira out of its territory.

Buldon lies near the former Camp Abubakar of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front and saw fighting from the 1970s to 2000. It also gave its name to the 1997 Buldon ceasefire agreement between the government and the MILF.

Datu Blah T. Sinsuat was once the western, coastal part of Upi, and is still informally called West Upi. It was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 198, which separated 12 barangays of Upi, including Kinimi, Matuber and Tambak, into a new town with its seat at Barangay Kinimi. Voters ratified it in a plebiscite in 2006.
The town is named after Datu Blah T. Sinsuat (1908 to 1981), who represented the area at the 1935 Constitutional Convention and served as Cotabato's representative in the 2nd Congress.

paragraphs: Datu Odin Sinsuat began as the town of Dinaig, one of the 10 municipalities that President Manuel Roxas organized in Cotabato province through Executive Order No. 82 in 1947. It was formed from the municipal districts of Dinaig, Awang and Salaman. In 1955 Republic Act No. 1248 separated the barrio of Upi to become its own town.

In 1994 the regional assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao renamed Dinaig as Datu Odin Sinsuat through Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 29. The town is home to Awang Airport and is the capital of Maguindanao del Norte.

sources.label: Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 29 (Lawphil, PDF)

paragraphs: Kabuntalan was first known as Tumbao. Executive Order No. 82 of 1947 annexed the municipal district of Tumbao to Cotabato, but Executive Order No. 227, signed on 16 June 1949, organized the former districts of Tumbao and Gambar into the Municipality of Tumbao.

Presidential Decree No. 1010 renamed it Kabuntalan in 1976 at the request of its officials and residents, in memory of the traditional leaders who held the title Sultan sa Kabuntalan. In 2006 Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 206 separated 11 of its barangays to form Northern Kabuntalan, and the town is sometimes called Mother Kabuntalan.

Matanog is one of the towns of the Iranun people in northern Maguindanao. It was created by Presidential Decree No. 780, signed by President Ferdinand Marcos on 25 August 1975, which separated 6 barangays from Parang, including Bayanga, Bugusan, Kidama and Sapad, without affecting Parang's existence.

Much of the area later formed part of Camp Abubakar, the main camp of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. Matanog was among the towns where fighting took place before the camp fell to government forces in 2000.

Northern Kabuntalan was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 206 of the regional assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. The act separated 11 barangays from Kabuntalan, among them Balong, Damatog, Libungan and Tumaguinting, and made Barangay Tumaguinting the seat of government. Voters ratified the new town in a plebiscite on 30 December 2006.

Parang was once part of the Sultanate of Maguindanao. In 1851 Spanish forces seized Polloc, now one of its barangays, and built a fort and naval base at its deep natural harbor. Under American rule, Polloc became part of the municipal district of Parang in 1917, and President Manuel Roxas organized Parang as a full municipality through Executive Order No. 82 in 1947.

Two towns were later carved from Parang: Buldon in 1961 under Republic Act No. 3419, and Matanog in 1975 under Presidential Decree No. 780. The Polloc Port, built in 1977, became a main port of the region, and in 2023 the Bangsamoro Parliament approved moving the regional seat of government to Parang.

The seat of the Sultanate of Maguindanao once stood within what is now Sultan Kudarat, near the Nuling Creek in Barangay Salimbao. The town was first known as Nuling, a municipal district that President Manuel Roxas organized into a municipality through Executive Order No. 82 in 1947, joining the districts of Nuling, Gubpangan and Balut.

Republic Act No. 5647 renamed Nuling as Sultan Kudarat on 21 June 1969, in honor of Mohammad Dipatuan Kudarat, Sultan of Maguindanao. From 1977 it served as the capital of Maguindanao province. In 1999 Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 89 separated 13 of its barangays to create Sultan Mastura, a change ratified in 2003.

sources.label: Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 89 (Lawphil, PDF)

paragraphs: Sultan Mastura, also known as Subpangen, was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 89 of 1999 of the regional assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. The act separated 13 barangays from Sultan Kudarat, including Boliok, Simuay Seashore and Tapayan, and made Barangay Tapayan the seat of government.
Voters ratified the new town in a plebiscite on 15 March 2003, and it began its corporate existence on 28 April 2003. It is named after Sultan Mastura, described as a son of Sultan Kudarat.

sources.label: Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 89 (Lawphil, PDF)

paragraphs: Talitay was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 52 of 1996 of the regional assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. The act formed the town from 13 barangays of Talayan, including Talitay, Kilalan and Gadungan, with Barangay Talitay as the seat of government. Voters approved the new town in a plebiscite in 1999.
In 2008 the regional assembly passed Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 228 to rename the town Sultan Sumagka, but no plebiscite on the change is on record and the name Talitay remains in use.

sources.label: Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 52 (Lawphil, PDF)

paragraphs: Upi is home to the Teduray, its native inhabitants. Its name probably comes from ufi, the Teduray name for the betel plant (Piper betel), which once grew there in abundance. In 1919 an American army officer, Captain Irving Edwards, founded the Upi Agricultural School in its valley.

Upi was a barrio of Dinaig, now Datu Odin Sinsuat, until Republic Act No. 1248, approved on 10 June 1955, made it a separate municipality. In 2006 its 12 coastal barangays were separated under Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 198 to form Datu Blah T. Sinsuat.

Ampatuan was created as a municipality of the old province of Cotabato by Republic Act No. 2509, approved in 1959, which separated 23 barrios from Datu Piang and set the seat of government at Decalungan. When Cotabato was divided in November 1973, Ampatuan became part of the new province of Maguindanao, while its barrio of Esperanza became a separate town in Sultan Kudarat.

In January 2004 voters approved the separation of 10 of its barangays to form Datu Abdullah Sangki. On 23 November 2009 the town was the site of the Maguindanao massacre, the killing of a convoy on its way to file a candidate's papers for the provincial governorship.

Buluan was one of 10 municipalities organized in the old province of Cotabato by Executive Order No. 82 of President Manuel Roxas in 1947, formed from the municipal districts of Buluan and Liguasan around Lake Buluan. Over the following decades its large territory gave rise to several towns, among them Tacurong, Columbio, Lutayan and President Quirino.

It became part of Maguindanao in 1973. Within the province, General Salipada K. Pendatun was carved from it in 1991, and Mangudadatu and Pandag in 2006. The provincial board named Buluan the capital of Maguindanao in 2014, and Republic Act No. 11550 of 2021 made it the capital of Maguindanao del Sur.

Datu Abdullah Sangki was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 153, passed by the regional legislative assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao and approved in August 2003. It was carved out of its mother town, Ampatuan, and its creation was ratified in a plebiscite on 3 January 2004. The law set the town's administrative centre at barangay Talisawa.
Datu Anggal Midtimbang is named after Datu Anggal Midtimbang, father of Datu Udzag Midtimbang, the first mayor of Talayan, and of other local leaders who later led Talayan and Guindulungan.

The town was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 207 of the regional legislature of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, taking 3 barangays from Talayan and 4 from Talitay. Voters ratified its creation in a plebiscite on 30 December 2006, and the law set its administrative centre at barangay Brar.

Datu Hoffer Ampatuan was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 220 of the regional legislature of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. It was formed from 9 barangays of Shariff Aguak and parts of 2 barangays of Datu Unsay, and its creation was ratified in a plebiscite on 30 July 2009, the same day the neighbouring towns of Shariff Saydona Mustapha and Datu Salibo were ratified.

Datu Paglas was created on 22 November 1973 by Presidential Decree No. 340 of President Ferdinand Marcos, issued on the day the old province of Cotabato was divided. The decree separated 7 barrios, Malala, Katil, Alip, Damawato, Manindolo, Puya and Sepaka, from the municipality of Columbio and placed the new town in the province of Maguindanao, with its seat of government at Alip. Columbio itself went to Sultan Kudarat.

The town lies at the old centre of the Sultanate of Buayan on the Rio Grande de Mindanao, a state that rivalled the Sultanate of Maguindanao. It was organized as the municipality of Dulawan by Executive Order No. 66 of President Manuel L. Quezon in 1936, one of the first municipalities of the old Cotabato province.

Republic Act No. 1035 of 1954 renamed it Datu Piang, after the influential Maguindanaon leader of the American colonial period. Its once large territory later gave rise to Ampatuan, Maganoy (now Shariff Aguak), Talayan, Datu Saudi-Ampatuan, Datu Salibo and Shariff Saydona Mustapha.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Datu Piang, Maguindanao del Sur

paragraphs: Datu Salibo was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 222, as amended by Act No. 253, of the regional legislature of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. It was formed from 4 whole barangays and parts of 10 others from Datu Piang, together with 2 whole barangays and part of another from Datu Saudi-Ampatuan. Its creation was ratified in a plebiscite held by the Commission on Elections on 30 July 2009.

Datu Saudi-Ampatuan is named after Datu Saudi Uy Ampatuan, a former mayor of Datu Piang who died in a bomb explosion in that town in December 2002. It was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 151 in July 2003, carved out of Datu Piang.
In July 2009 parts of its territory went to the newly created towns of Shariff Saydona Mustapha and Datu Salibo, following plebiscites on Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Acts No. 225 and 222.
Datu Unsay was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 150 in July 2003, carved out of the municipality of Shariff Aguak. It is named after its former mayor, Andal "Datu Unsay" Ampatuan Jr.

In July 2009, with the ratification of Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Acts No. 225 and 220, 2 of its barangays and parts of 2 others were transferred to the new towns of Shariff Saydona Mustapha and Datu Hoffer Ampatuan.

The town is named after Salipada K. Pendatun (1912 to 1985), a lawyer from Pikit, Cotabato, who led guerrilla forces in Mindanao during the Second World War and later served in Congress and the Batasang Pambansa.

It was created on 7 April 1991 by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 3, which carved it out of Buluan. It was the first local government unit created by the regional assembly of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. In 2001, 4 of its barangays were separated to form the municipality of Paglat.

sources.label: Wikipedia: General Salipada K. Pendatun, Maguindanao del Sur

paragraphs: Guindulungan was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 139 in March 2003, carved out of the municipality of Talayan. Its first appointed mayor was Hadji Datu Midpantao M. Midtimbang Sr., a religious leader who had also served as mayor of Talayan and as vice governor of Maguindanao. Its people are overwhelmingly Maguindanaon.

Mamasapano was once a barangay of Shariff Aguak. It became a municipality under Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 54, with 18 barangays taken from Shariff Aguak, after a plebiscite on 31 October 1998. In July 2009 it gave up 4 barangays and part of another to the new town of Shariff Saydona Mustapha.

On 25 January 2015 the area was the site of the Mamasapano clash, in which 44 members of the Philippine National Police Special Action Force were killed in fighting with armed groups, an event that strained the peace process with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front.

Mangudadatu was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 204 of the regional legislature of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. It was formed from 8 barangays in the southern part of Buluan, and its creation was ratified in a plebiscite on 30 December 2006, the same day as the neighbouring town of Pandag, which was also carved from Buluan.

Pagagawan was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 95 in July 2000, carved out of the municipality of Pagalungan. Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 152 of 2003 renamed it Datu Montawal, and the municipal, provincial and regional governments use that name, as does Republic Act No. 11550 of 2021. No record has been found of a plebiscite confirming the renaming, however, so the Commission on Elections and the Philippine Statistics Authority still list it as Pagagawan.

The name Pagalungan is a Maguindanaon word for "mirror", said to come from a deep, clear pond that women of the place used as one. Pagalungan became a municipality in 1947 under Executive Order No. 82 of President Manuel Roxas, which organized 10 new municipalities in the old province of Cotabato. It was formed from the municipal districts of Pikit-Pagalungan, Silik and Balatikan.
It became part of Maguindanao in 1973. In 2000 part of its territory was separated to form Pagagawan, now known locally as Datu Montawal.

Paglat was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 112 in 2001, carved out of 4 barangays of General Salipada K. Pendatun, a town that had itself been carved out of Buluan in 1991. Bai Zulaika Pendatun-Langkuno was first appointed mayor, but her appointment was recalled by then regional governor Nur Misuari in favour of Datu Conte Mangelen.

sources.label: Wikipedia: General Salipada K. Pendatun, Maguindanao del Sur

paragraphs: Pandag was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 203 of the regional legislature of the Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao. It was formed from 8 barangays in the northern part of Buluan, and its creation was ratified in a plebiscite on 30 December 2006, the same day as Mangudadatu, which was carved from Buluan's southern barangays.
Rajah Buayan takes its name from the Sultanate of Buayan. The area, previously known as Sapakan, became the capital of Buayan during the reign of Datu Uto around 1875.

The modern municipality was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 166 of October 2002 and ratified in a plebiscite on 4 September 2004. It was carved out of Sultan sa Barongis, which gave up 11 of its barangays to the new town.

Shariff Aguak was founded as Maganoy by Executive Order No. 47 of President Diosdado Macapagal in 1963, which formed the new town from 28 barrios of Datu Piang in the old province of Cotabato. Maganoy was the legal capital of Maguindanao from 1973 until 1977, when the seat was moved to Sultan Kudarat, and it later served as the working capital under several governors from the town.
Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 45 renamed it Shariff Aguak in 1996. It later lost territory to Mamasapano, Datu Unsay, Datu Hoffer Ampatuan and Shariff Saydona Mustapha.

The town is named after Shariff Saydona Mustapha, an Arab missionary from Mecca who arrived in mainland Mindanao in the mid-15th century. He was a paternal uncle of Shariff Kabungsuwan, the first Sultan of Maguindanao, and is regarded as an ancestor of the Ampatuan, Mangacop, Masukat and Sangki clans.

It was created by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 225, as amended by Act No. 252, from barangays of Shariff Aguak, Mamasapano, Datu Unsay, Datu Piang and Datu Saudi-Ampatuan, and was ratified in a plebiscite on 30 July 2009.

South Upi was created on 22 September 1976 by Presidential Decree No. 1011 of President Ferdinand Marcos. The decree detached 11 barangays, including Looy, Bongo, Biarong, Lamud, Kigan and Pandan, from the municipality of Upi in Maguindanao to form the new town, without affecting the existence of Upi itself.

Sultan sa Barongis was created as the municipality of Lambayong by Executive Order No. 543 of President Elpidio Quirino in October 1952, formed from places in and around the barrios of Barurao and Lambayong in the municipality of Dulawan, now Datu Piang.

Republic Act No. 2587 of 1959 changed its name to Sultan sa Barongis, honouring Mantagmama of the House of Talik, grandfather of Salipada K. Pendatun. In 2004, 11 of its barangays were transferred to the new municipality of Rajah Buayan.

Talayan was created by Presidential Decree No. 1009 of President Ferdinand Marcos in 1976. The decree separated former barrios of Datu Piang, among them Talayan, Brar and Midtimbang, together with barrios of Dinaig, now Datu Odin Sinsuat, including Talitay, to form the new municipality in Maguindanao.
Datu Udzag Midtimbang was its first appointed mayor. The original Talayan has since been divided into 4 municipalities: Talayan, Talitay, Datu Anggal Midtimbang and Guindulungan.

Kadayangan was created by Bangsamoro Autonomy Act 42, which the Bangsamoro Parliament passed on 17 August 2023. It joins 7 barangays that had belonged to Midsayap, North Cotabato, and voted to join the Bangsamoro region in the 2019 plebiscite: Central Labas, Kapinpilan, Malingao, Mudseng, Sambulawan, Tugal and Tumbras. The act names Kapinpilan as the seat of government.

Voters in the 7 barangays ratified the act in a plebiscite on 13 April 2024. On 13 July 2024, officers-in-charge appointed by Chief Minister Ahod Balawag Ebrahim took their oath to run the new town until its first elected officials took office after the May 2025 elections.

paragraphs: Bongao has some of the oldest traces of human presence in Southeast Asia: bones, jars and shells found at the Balobok Rock Shelter have been dated to between 8,810 and 5,190 years ago, and the site was declared an Important Cultural Treasure in 2017. For centuries the area was a centre of Sama-Bajau culture and later came under the Sultanate of Sulu.

Bongao was a municipal district of Sulu until Executive Order No. 355, issued by President Carlos P. Garcia in 1959, made it a municipality effective 1 July 1958. In 1973 Presidential Decree No. 302 placed it in the new Province of Tawi-Tawi. The provincial capital, first set at Batu-Batu, was later moved to Bongao, which grew into the province's centre of government and trade.

Languyan was created by Presidential Decree No. 1086 on 4 February 1977. The decree detached 11 barangays, among them Languyan Proper, Darussalam, Maraning and Tumahubong, from the municipalities of Bongao, Tandubas and South Ubian to form the new town, with its seat of government at Languyan Proper. The decree gave as its purposes faster development and rehabilitation, a government closer to residents, and support for peace and order in the area. Languyan lies on the mainland of Tawi-Tawi Island.

Mapun is the home of the Jama Mapun, whose language is Pullun Mapun. Long known as Cagayan de Sulu, the island was a source of rice and sago for the Sulu Archipelago and traded with British Borneo. Through an oversight in the 1898 Treaty of Paris, it stayed under Spain until it was ceded to the United States under the Treaty of Washington, ratified in 1901.

Executive Order No. 355 made Cagayan de Sulu a municipality of Sulu effective 1 July 1958, and Presidential Decree No. 302 moved it to the new Province of Tawi-Tawi in 1973. Batas Pambansa Blg. 647 renamed it Cagayan de Tawi-Tawi in 1984, and Republic Act No. 6672 gave it its present name, Mapun, on 5 September 1988.

Panglima Sugala was formerly the municipality of Balimbing, a Sulu municipal district made a municipality by Executive Order No. 355 effective 1 July 1958. When Presidential Decree No. 302 created the Province of Tawi-Tawi in 1973, it named Bato-Bato (Batu-Batu) in Balimbing as the provincial capital. The capital was later transferred to Bongao, in 1979 according to Wikipedia.
Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 7, enacted on 4 July 1991 and approved by the Regional Governor on 9 September 1991, renamed Balimbing as Panglima Sugala.

Sapa-Sapa was created by Presidential Decree No. 1087 on 4 February 1977. The decree detached 15 barangays of Tandubas, among them Sapa-Sapa, Baldatal Islam, Lakit-Lakit and Malanta, to form the new municipality, with its seat of government at Barangay Sapa-Sapa. The decree said residents had asked for the new town, and that it was meant to make local government more efficient and help the community become self-reliant.

Sibutu Island was historically part of the Sitangkai island group, a traditional home of the Sama and Bajau peoples on the sea trade routes to Borneo. Through an oversight in the 1898 Treaty of Paris, Sibutu stayed under Spain until it was ceded to the United States under the Treaty of Washington, ratified in 1901.

The municipality was created out of Sitangkai by Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 197, ratified in a plebiscite on 21 October 2006, which moved 16 Sitangkai barangays on Sibutu Island to the new town. Presidential Proclamation No. 691 declared 21 October 2024 a special non-working day to mark the anniversary.
Simunul is the site of the Sheikh Karimul Makhdum Mosque, regarded as the first mosque built in the Philippines and declared a National Historical Landmark. Most of its people are Muslim.

Simunul was a municipal district of Sulu until Executive Order No. 355, issued by President Carlos P. Garcia in 1959, made it a municipality effective 1 July 1958. In 1973 Presidential Decree No. 302 moved it from Sulu to the newly created Province of Tawi-Tawi.

Sitangkai, the southernmost town in the Philippines, is a traditional home of the Sama and Bajau peoples on the old sea trade routes to Borneo. Its local datus traced descent from the royal houses of Sulu, Sabah and Sarawak, and in the early 1900s Tausug settlers began arriving. Because people travel by boat between houses linked by footbridges, it is called the "Venice of the South".

Executive Order No. 355 made Sitangkai a municipality of Sulu effective 1 July 1958, and Presidential Decree No. 302 moved it to Tawi-Tawi in 1973. In 2006 Muslim Mindanao Autonomy Act No. 197 transferred 16 of its 25 barangays, all on Sibutu Island, to the new municipality of Sibutu.

South Ubian was a municipal district of Sulu until Executive Order No. 355 made it a municipality effective 1 July 1958. In 1973 Presidential Decree No. 302 moved it to the new Province of Tawi-Tawi, and in 1977 Presidential Decree No. 1086 detached some of its barangays, together with parts of Bongao and Tandubas, to form Languyan.

The town includes Tabawan, a Sama island village with ancestral houses and cultural practices protected by Municipal Ordinance No. 14-2020 and put forward for the Philippines' tentative list of UNESCO World Heritage sites.

Tandubas takes its name from the Malay "Tanjung Bas", which local accounts say means a place of landing, after traders who settled on the island; in Sama, "tanjung" became "tandu". The island was part of the Sultanate of Sulu.

Executive Order No. 355 made Tandubas a municipality of Sulu effective 1 July 1958, covering areas that are now Sapa-Sapa and part of Languyan. Presidential Decree No. 302 moved it to the new Province of Tawi-Tawi in 1973. On 4 February 1977, Presidential Decree No. 1087 created Sapa-Sapa entirely from Tandubas barangays, and Presidential Decree No. 1086 took others to form Languyan.

The Turtle Islands, of which Taganak is the largest, passed to the United States under the treaties ending Spanish rule, but were run by the British North Borneo Company. A 1930 treaty confirmed them as Philippine territory, and the Philippines took over their administration on 16 October 1947. A dispute over the Taganak lighthouse followed.

Executive Order No. 355 made Turtle Islands a municipality of Sulu effective 1 July 1958, and Presidential Decree No. 302 moved it to Tawi-Tawi in 1973. Proclamation No. 171 of 1999 declared the town and its surrounding waters the Turtle Islands Wildlife Sanctuary.
